extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of English drama and playwriting (particularly Restoration comedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for composing and evaluating Restoration-era comedy and stagecraft — covers plot construction, character choice, tone (humour vs love), audience tailoring, decorum, and actorly embodiment of comic roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of plots, choice of characters, and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: "height and accuracy of judgment in the ordering of his plots, his choice of characters, and maintaining what he had chosen to the end."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for Jonson's strengths: judges should value careful plot ordering, thoughtful choice of characters, and fidelity to the chosen design throughout a play. Consistency of chosen elements to the end is a mark of good dramatic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of love as foundation of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: "love, which is the foundation of all comedies in other languages, is scarcely mentioned in any of his plays."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical expectation (in non-English traditions) that love should be central to comedy; absence of a love-plot is noted as a deficiency relative to continental models. Writers should consider whether a love-plot is appropriate for comedic energy and audience expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of comic targets to audience (humour vs meanness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the poets of this age will be more wary than to imitate the meanness of his persons. Gentlemen will now be entertained with the follies of each other; and, though they allow Cobb and Tib to speak properly, yet they are not much pleased with their tankard, or with their rags."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid depicting genteel characters in undignified, vulgar ways that would repel a more refined audience. Choose comic targets and social types that the intended audience can laugh at without feeling offended; adapt levels of 'meanness' to contemporary tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor predecessors without servile imitation; adapt to contemporary manners
rubrics_metrics.description: "render to our predecessors what is their due, without confining ourselves to a servile imitation of all they writ... ascribe to the gallantry and civility of our age the advantage which we have above them"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A balanced approach: acknowledge and learn from earlier writers, but do not slavishly copy them. Embrace present manners, civility, and fashions where they better please contemporary audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to decorum and French-influenced refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations on "the refinement which our stage had now borrowed from the French" and that in some earlier ages extravagance might be tolerated rather than an offence against the "decorum of the scene."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an expectation of decorum (proper behavior onstage) influenced by French dramatic rules; writers should avoid actions, lines, or extravagances that violate the accepted decorum of the scene, especially when addressing refined audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor complexity and artfulness to your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "Art was not demanded... incapable of receiving the delights which a cultivated mind derives from the gradual developement of a story, the just dependence of its parts upon each other, the minute beauties of language, and the absence of every thing incongruous or indecorous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing for a cultivated, courtly audience, employ gradual story development, careful dependence of parts, subtle language, and removal of incongruity. For popular audiences of small theatres, prioritize more direct emotional effects and broader, immediate appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address judgment vs. feelings depending on audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "He was to address himself to the heads and judgments of his audience, ... not to their feelings..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the audience is learned or courtly, craft plays to appeal to intellect, taste, and critical judgment (wit, structure, refinement). For popular audiences, aim more at stirring feeling and dramatic immediacy. Choose rhetorical aim accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value natural spontaneity and allowable irregularity
rubrics_metrics.description: "we may rejoice that he purchased, at so slight a sacrifice, the power and privilege of launching into every subject with a liberty as unbounded as his genius; ... As there is music, uninformed by art, In those wild notes... which better taught at home, yet please us less."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some irregularities in structure or diction can be virtues if they yield natural, original, and powerful expression. Do not eliminate every 'irregularity' if it enables imaginative force or genuine emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifics of comic acting and characterization (Melantha example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cibber's account: Melantha is "as finished an impertinent as ever fluttered in a drawing-room... Her language, dress, motion, manners, soul, and body, are in a continual hurry to be something more than is necessary or commendable... the first ridiculous airs... reads the letter... crumbles it at once into her palm... pours down upon him her whole artillery of airs, eyes, and motion; down goes her dainty diving body... launches into a flood of fine language... playing her chest forward in fifty falls and risings, like a swan upon waving water."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For actors and playwrights: create roles with integrated verbal and physical characteristics (speech, costume, gesture, posture, timing). Successful portrayal requires detailed physical beats, expressive gestures, and sustained comic energy; precise staging and diction amplify comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware abrupt or contrived turns of fortune (tragic subplot)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sudden turn of fortune in the conclusion is ridiculed in 'The Rehearsal.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sudden, unearned reversals or contrived conclusions (especially when mixing tragic elements into comedy), since they invite ridicule and undermine credibility. Plot reversals should be foreshadowed and motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreign phrases when naturalized
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of the French phrases, which the affected lady throws into her conversation, some have been since naturalized, as 'good graces', 'minuet', 'chagrin', 'grimace', 'ridicule', and others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating foreign terms (e.g., French phrases) can lend contemporary color and social realism, but they should be integrated naturally so they don't jar the audience or seem forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging and audience composition shape writing choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of small, popular theatres in Shakespeare's day versus court-patronized stages in Dryden's; "It was a natural consequence, that the writings of these great men were biassed by the taste of those, for whom they wrote" and "Dryden... wrote for a stage patronized by a monarch and his courtiers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider theatre size, venue, and audience makeup when choosing language register, plot complexity, and types of characters. What pleases a crowded, popular venue differs from what pleases a courtly, critical audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production/promotional practices can shape reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologue and stage-practice notes: using masking balls and courtly entertainments to recommend a play; "For that's one way, howe'er the play fall short, To oblige the town, the city, and the court."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-textual production choices — entertainments, social events, and hospitality associated with performances — affect public reception and can be used to bolster a play's success; writers and producers should coordinate publicity/staging to reach intended patrons.
